citations.quote:
Fix a coordinate orientation-reversing reflection $r:S^3\to S^3$ for the mirror convention. Let $K$ and $J$ be smooth oriented knots in the standard oriented three-sphere. A connected-sum datum consists of one smoothly embedded closed three-ball around a short subarc of $K$ and one around a short subarc of $J$, each meeting its knot in a single trivial properly embedded arc, together with the fixed standard orientation-reversing boundary identification of the two standard oriented ball boundaries that joins the oriented arcs into one circle. Choose this standard map once in the standard two-ball model so that it commutes with $r$ and an orientation-preserving half-turn interchanging the two balls preserves the joining convention. Here a trivial arc is an embedded interval in a ball that is carried by an orientation-preserving diffeomorphism of ball-arc pairs to a straight diameter. Remove the interiors of the two balls and glue the remaining boundary spheres using this fixed identification; the resulting oriented knot in the standard oriented three-sphere is a connected sum of $K$ and $J$, denoted $K\#J$ for the specified datum.

The **standard unknot** is the oriented unit circle in a fixed coordinate two-plane of $S^3\subset\mathbb R^4$. A knot is **nontrivial** if it is not ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms of $S^3$ to the standard unknot. A nontrivial knot is **prime** if it has no connected-sum presentation whose two summand knots are both nontrivial.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $F$ be a compact smooth surface with boundary, let $M$ be a smooth three-manifold without boundary, and let $S\subset M$ be a closed embedded smooth surface. If $i:F\to M$ is a smooth embedding whose boundary restriction $i|_{\partial F}$ is transverse to $S$, then there is a smooth isotopy $i_t:F\to M$ through embeddings, fixed on a neighbourhood of $\partial F$, such that $i_1(F)$ is transverse to $S$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Assume countable choice. Let $S\subset S^3$ be the image of a smooth embedding of the standard $S^2$. There is a smooth ambient isotopy $H_t:S^3\to S^3$, with $H_0=\operatorname{id}$, such that $H_1(S)$ is the standard equatorial sphere $E$. In particular $S^3\setminus S$ has exactly two components. Their closures $B_+$ and $B_-$ are smoothly embedded standard closed $3$-balls with common boundary $S$. If $D_+$ and $D_-$ denote the standard closed hemispheres bounded by $E$, the labels can be chosen so that the restrictions $H_1:B_\pm\to D_\pm$ are diffeomorphisms with the same boundary restriction $H_1|_S:S\to E$. Thus the ball identifications are compatible on their boundary and on a common two-sided collar of that boundary.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]]). Let $S$ be an oriented Hausdorff $C^2$ surface without boundary, possibly disconnected. Then:

1. Every compact subset $K\subset S$ lies in the interior of a compact finitely cellulated $C^2$ subsurface $N$. If $K$ is contained in one connected component of $S$, $N$ can be chosen connected. A specified finite embedded regular $C^2$ graph contained in $\operatorname{Int}N$ can be included in its one-skeleton.
2. Every connected closed compact subsurface has an oriented genus normal form: the sphere for $g=0$, or the polygon word $\prod_{i=1}^g a_i b_i a_i^{-1}b_i^{-1}$ for $g\ge1$, with $\chi=2-2g$. A connected compact subsurface with $b>0$ boundary circles has a free fundamental group; capping its boundaries defines genus $g$ and gives $\chi=2-2g-b$ and free rank $2g+b-1$.
3. The fundamental group of every connected component of $S$ is torsion-free.
4. Every regular embedded $C^2$ nullhomotopic circle $c$ bounds an embedded compact disk region in $S$. Here a disk region is a compact subsurface homeomorphic to the closed disk, with boundary exactly $c$; its inherited surface structure and boundary are $C^2$. It is unique unless the **connected component containing $c$** is a sphere; in that component the two complementary disk regions are the two possibilities.

The normal forms in clause 2 are homeomorphism normal forms. No general differentiable smoothing theorem or arbitrary-surface triangulation-existence theorem is a premise of this item.

derivations.claim: Take a smooth spanning disk $E$ for $K$ from [F1] and make it transverse to $S$ using [F2]. Its intersection with $S$ is a compact one-manifold with boundary exactly the two points $K\cap S$. Consequently it consists of one proper arc $\alpha\subset E$ and finitely many circles. Indeed every compact one-manifold has finitely many interval and circle components, and precisely one interval is needed to account for these two boundary points.

If circles occur, choose a circle $c$ bounding a disk $Q\subset S$ whose interior contains neither $\alpha$ nor another intersection circle. Such a choice exists by finite nesting. The disjoint circles cut the sphere into regions with a tree as dual graph: each additional separating circle splits one region in two. Root this tree at the region containing the connected arc $\alpha$ and take a leaf other than the root. Its closure is the required disk $Q$, using the sphere disk regions in [F4]. Thus $\operatorname{int}Q\cap E=\varnothing$ and $Q\cap K=\varnothing$. The circle $c$ also bounds a subdisk $E_c$ in the interior of $E$. This subdisk misses $\alpha$, since $\alpha$ is connected, disjoint from $c$ and has its endpoints on $\partial E$.

Replace $E_c$ by a nearby parallel copy of $Q$, keeping the component with the original boundary $K$. This yields another embedded spanning disk. To see this locally, the interior of $Q$ misses $E$ by step 2.1; push it a sufficiently small distance to the side of $S$ containing the retained collar of $E\setminus E_c$, and join it to that collar in product coordinates along $c$. The push and corner rounding introduce no intersection with $S$ or with the retained disk. Outside this collar everything is unchanged. The operation removes $c$ and any intersection circles in $E_c$, introduces none, and preserves $\alpha$. Repeating finitely often produces an embedded spanning disk, still denoted $E$, with $E\cap S=\alpha$. No assertion that these disk replacements are ambient isotopies is needed.

Cut this disk along $\alpha$. By [F4] there are two disks, each bounded by $\alpha$ and one of the two arcs into which $K\cap S$ divides $K$. Their interiors miss $S$. Near $\alpha$, transversality places the two disk interiors on opposite sides of $S$; connectedness keeps each interior on its respective side. By [F3] these are the two balls $B_1,B_2$, and the corresponding boundary arcs of $K$ are $a_1,a_2$. The two cut disks are therefore the required $E_i$, with $b_i=\alpha$ on their common boundary sphere. Local endpoint coordinates provide the stated corner convention.

citations.quote: Assume countable choice. Let $K\subset S^3$ be a smooth unknot and let $S\subset S^3$ be a smoothly embedded sphere transverse to $K$ in exactly two points. Write $B_1,B_2$ for its closed ball sides and $a_i=K\cap B_i$. For each $i$ there is an embedded disk $E_i\subset B_i$ with boundary $a_i\cup b_i$, where $b_i\subset S$ is a simple arc with the same endpoints as $a_i$, and $\operatorname{int}E_i\subset\operatorname{int}B_i$. Thus both ball arcs are boundary-parallel. Disks and arcs may have the usual rounded corners at the two endpoints.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For an oriented smooth knot $K\subset S^3$, define

$$\mathcal G(K):=\{n\in\mathbb N_0: \text{there is a Seifert surface }F\text{ for }K\text{ with }g(F)=n\}.$$

Every element of $\mathcal G(K)$ is the genus of a connected compact oriented surface. The existence theorem makes $\mathcal G(K)$ nonempty, and the well-ordering of $\mathbb N_0$ gives its least element. The **smooth knot genus** is $g(K):=\min\mathcal G(K)$. This genus is the minimum over embedded spanning surfaces; it is not the number of Seifert circles or the genus of every surface produced from a diagram.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. For every smooth oriented knot $K$ in $S^3$, its Seifert genus is zero if and only if $K$ is ambient isotopic through orientation-preserving diffeomorphisms to the standard unknot.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

1. **Compact main case.** Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold, possibly with boundary, let $N$ be a smooth manifold without boundary, let $F:M\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings that is constant near the ends of $I$, and let $W$ be an open neighbourhood of $F(M\times I)$ in $N$. Then there is an ambient isotopy $H:N\times I\to N$ with $H_0=\mathrm{id}_N$, every $H_t$ a diffeomorphism, $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ for all $t\in I$, $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ outside $W$ for every $t$, and $H_t$ stationary near the ends; if $F$ is constant near the ends with parameter $\varepsilon$, then $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ for $t\le\varepsilon/2$ and $H_t=H_1$ for $t\ge1-\varepsilon/2$.
2. **Relative form.** Let $N$ be boundaryless, $U\subseteq N$ open, $A\subseteq U$ compact, and let $F:U\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings whose track image is open in $N\times I$. Then there is a compactly supported ambient isotopy $H$ of $N$ with $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ on a neighbourhood of $A$ for every $t$.
3. **Boundary stratum.** If $N$ has boundary and $F(M\times I)\subseteq\partial N$, then the ambient isotopy of clause 1 can be chosen with every $H_t$ carrying $\partial N$ onto itself; if $F(M\times I)\subseteq N\setminus\partial N$, it can be chosen compactly supported in $N\setminus\partial N$.
4. **General isotopies.** For the same compact source (possibly with boundary) and boundaryless target as in clause 1, every smooth isotopy extends with support in a compact subset of any prescribed neighbourhood $W$ of $F(M\times I)$. The endpoint-constancy hypothesis and the stationary-end conclusion are both omitted; all other conclusions of clause 1 hold.

derivations.claim: Every circle component of either factor remains a circle component of $T$. Thus if $T$ is trivial neither factor has a circle; if both factors are trivial the sum has none. It remains to analyze the single arcs and their boundary-parallelism disks. Write $p$ for the common arc endpoint in $D$, and $x_i$ for the remaining endpoint on the unglued part of $\partial B_i$.

Suppose the total arc $a=a_1\cup a_2$ is boundary-parallel, with disk $E$ and boundary arc $b\subset\partial B$. Close $a$ by pushing the interior of $b$ just outside $B$. The disk $E$, extended across the thin boundary collar, gives a smooth spanning disk for the resulting knot $K$, so [F2] makes $K$ an unknot. The sphere $\partial B_i$, rounded along $\partial D$ away from $p$, meets $K$ exactly at $p$ and $x_i$: the pushed cap lies outside $B$ except for its endpoint collars. Smooth these endpoint collars transversely. Its portion inside $B_i$ is precisely $a_i$ up to these arbitrarily short collar adjustments. By [F1] it is boundary-parallel in $B_i$. Undoing the collar adjustment transports its disk back to $a_i$. Together with step 1.1 this proves triviality of both factors.

Conversely assume both arcs are boundary-parallel, and choose disks $E_i$ with boundary $a_i\cup b_i$. Fix a point $q\in\partial D$ away from the endpoints and a simple arc $\lambda\subset D$ from $p$ to $q$. On each $\partial B_i$, choose a simple boundary arc $b_i'$ from $p$ to $x_i$ which follows $\lambda$ in $D$ and otherwise lies in the unglued boundary disk. Any two simple arcs in a sphere with these two fixed endpoints are isotopic relative to the endpoints. To check the endpoint issue, remove small endpoint disks and straighten the arc germs. The intervening surface is an annulus; two spanning arcs differ by an integer winding, removed by rotating one endpoint disk through that many full turns while fixing its center. After this adjustment, remove finitely many innermost bigons and slide the remaining disjoint arcs across their disk, using [F4]. Thus an isotopy takes $b_i$ to $b_i'$ and fixes $p,x_i$, although it need not fix their neighborhoods.

Extend this boundary isotopy to the ball fixing $a_i$ pointwise. Here is the relative collar construction. At an endpoint use coordinates $(x,y,z)$ with the boundary $z=0$ and $a_i$ the positive $z$-axis. The time-dependent boundary field vanishes at $(0,0)$; extend it independently of $z$ there, so that it vanishes along $a_i$. Away from these charts take a sufficiently thin boundary collar missing the remaining compact interior subarc, and extend with a cutoff. Patch the finitely many extensions by a partition of unity; they have the same prescribed boundary values and all vanish along $a_i$. Their compactly supported flow gives the claimed extension, in the relative form of [F3]. It transports $E_i$ to a boundary-parallelism disk with boundary $a_i\cup b_i'$. The two transported disks meet exactly along $\lambda$: their interiors lie in the disjoint ball interiors and their other boundary arcs lie on the unglued boundary pieces.

Glue these disks along $\lambda$ and round the seam. Two disks joined along one boundary interval form a disk, as can be checked by flattening that interval and its two half-disk collars. Its boundary is $a_1\cup a_2$ together with the two remaining boundary arcs joined at $q$, which form an arc in $\partial B$. Along the interior of $\lambda$ the glued disk lies in the interior of $B$, and all other interior points already lie in the ball interiors. It is therefore a boundary-parallelism disk for the total arc. Step 1.1 excludes circle components, so $T$ is trivial. Together with step 2.1 this proves the equivalence and both stated consequences.

Assume countable choice. Let $B=B_1\cup_D B_2\subset S^3$ be a supplied smooth boundary sum of two embedded balls along a disk, with corners rounded. In each $B_i$ let $T_i$ consist of one proper smooth arc $a_i$ and finitely many disjoint interior circles. Suppose $T_i\cap D$ is just one endpoint of $a_i$, matched to the corresponding endpoint in the other disk. The union is a one-string ball tangle $T\subset B$. Call such a tangle trivial if it has no circle components and its proper arc cobounds an embedded disk with an arc in the boundary sphere, with disk interior in the ball interior.

Then $T$ is trivial if and only if both $T_1$ and $T_2$ are trivial. In particular, a nontrivial factor makes the boundary sum nontrivial, and a nontrivial boundary sum has a nontrivial factor.

derivations.claim: By [F3], the boundary circle of $D$ cuts $S$ into the disks $Q_1,Q_2$ specified in the statement. The embedded unions $Q_i\cup D$ are spheres with corners along $\partial D$. Round them in a product neighborhood of that circle, away from $L$, and use nearby parallel copies of $D$ when considering both spheres simultaneously. Each sphere meets $L$ at its one original point $x_i$ and its one new meridional point near $p$. No other link intersection occurs because $D$ has precisely the one supplied intersection and the rounding collar misses $L$.

Cutting $B$ along $D$ gives two ball sides $B_1,B_2$, with boundaries the rounded $Q_i\cup D$. Here the ball assertion follows from [F1], rather than from an assumption that every disk is already standard. For the sphere $Q_i\cup D$, the connected open set exterior to $B$ is disjoint from it and lies in one complementary component. The other complementary component is contained in $B$, and its closure is a ball by [F1]. In $\operatorname{int}B$ the two sphere complements are separated precisely by $\operatorname{int}D$: a path crossing between their local sides must cross that disk. Thus these two interior ball regions exhaust the cut ball, and their boundaries meet along the copy of $D$. Restoring its collar identifies $B$ with their boundary sum along $D$.

The original proper arc of $L\cap B$ has endpoints $x_1,x_2$ on opposite boundary disks and crosses $D$ exactly once. Its two portions therefore give one proper arc in each $B_i$, joining $x_i$ to the new endpoint near $p$. Each closed component misses $D$ and stays in one ball. Consequently $L\cap B$ is precisely the boundary sum of the two child one-string tangles. Since the original side was nontrivial, [F2] implies that at least one child tangle, say the one in $B_i$, is nontrivial.

The complementary ball side of $Q_i\cup D$ is the rounded union of $B_0$ and the other child ball $B_j$, glued along $Q_j$, where $\{i,j\}=\{1,2\}$. Indeed $B_0$ is outside the original $B$, while $B_j$ is its remaining part; their common boundary disk is $Q_j$. Their link arcs meet that disk only at $x_j$, and their union is the complementary side tangle. This is a supplied boundary sum in the sense of [F2]; its total manifold is a ball by [F1] applied to $Q_i\cup D$. The factor in $B_0$ is the original opposite nontrivial side. Hence [F2] makes this complementary side tangle nontrivial as well.

The child sphere indexed by $i$ meets $L$ twice by step 1.1, has the nontrivial inside tangle from step 3.1 and the nontrivial outside tangle from step 4.1. It is therefore a nontrivial decomposing sphere. Deleting its two meridional cap disks gives the corresponding nontrivial decomposing annulus. This proves exactly the asserted survival under the supplied meridional surgery, without asserting that the child is isotopic to the original sphere.

derivations.claim: Choose a boundary circle $C$ of a nondisk component $P$ of $F$ and a sufficiently close interior parallel $c\subset P$. The circle $c$ does not bound a disk in $F$: its annular collar with $C$, together with such a disk, would give a disk component with boundary $C$, which must exhaust the connected component $P$, contrary to its choice. Parametrize the supplied ball by the standard ball. The circle $C$ bounds a disk $R$ on its boundary sphere by [F3], since stereographic projection from a point outside $C$ gives a planar linear nullhomotopy. A sufficiently short inward collar from [F1] can be chosen tangent to $F$ along $\partial F$: in its neat half-plane coordinates choose an inward field tangent to $F$, patch these finitely many local fields near $\partial F$, and extend it to the boundary collar. Thus the inward parallel copy $Q$ of $R$ has boundary $c$, lies otherwise in $\operatorname{int}B$, and near $c$ meets $F$ just along its boundary.

Make the interior of $Q$ transverse to $F$ while keeping its collar of $c$ fixed. One way to apply [F2] literally is to double the ball and the neat surface across their product boundary collars. The double of $F$ is a closed smooth embedded surface in the doubled ball. Remove a smaller boundary collar of $Q$; the resulting disk boundary is disjoint from the doubled surface and hence transverse. Apply [F2] to this smaller disk and reattach the unchanged collar. A sufficiently small perturbation stays in the interior of $B$. The result has intersection with $F$ equal to $c$ and finitely many interior circles: the intersections form a compact transverse one-manifold away from the boundary collar, with no endpoints there.

If an interior intersection circle bounds a disk in $F$, select such a disk whose interior misses $Q$. This is possible by finite nesting: inside any disk bounded by an inessential intersection circle, every intersection circle also bounds its inner disk there; choose an innermost one. The curve $c$ cannot lie in this disk, because it is essential in $F$ by step 1.1. Denote the selected disk by $A$ and its boundary by $d$. Surger $Q$ along two nearby copies of $A$, retain the disk with original boundary $c$ and discard the sphere. The interior of $A$ misses $Q$, so the result is embedded. Near $d$ push the retained copy of $A$ to the side of $F$ containing the retained collar of $Q\setminus d$ and round the seam. This removes $d$ and any intersection circles discarded with the other component and introduces none; the pushed disk is disjoint from $F$. It leaves the boundary collar of $Q$ unchanged. Repeating decreases the finite number of interior circles strictly, so after finitely many surgeries none of the remaining interior circles bounds a disk in $F$.

If an interior intersection circle remains, choose one innermost on the auxiliary disk $Q$. Its inner subdisk $X$ has interior disjoint from $F$, lies in $\operatorname{int}B$, and has boundary not bounding a disk in $F$ by step 3.1. It is the required compression. If no interior circle remains, use $X=Q$: its interior misses $F$, and its boundary is the essential curve $c$ from step 1.1. In both cases a geometric compressing disk for $F$ has been constructed.

citations.quote: An oriented link $L\subset S^3$ is **split** if a smoothly embedded sphere $S\subset S^3\setminus L$ has link points in both components of $S^3\setminus S$; otherwise $L$ is **nonsplit**.

Assume countable choice. Let $S\subset S^3$ be the image of a smooth embedding of the standard $S^2$. There is a smooth ambient isotopy $H_t:S^3\to S^3$, with $H_0=\operatorname{id}$, such that $H_1(S)$ is the standard equatorial sphere $E$. In particular $S^3\setminus S$ has exactly two components. Their closures $B_+$ and $B_-$ are smoothly embedded standard closed $3$-balls with common boundary $S$. If $D_+$ and $D_-$ denote the standard closed hemispheres bounded by $E$, the labels can be chosen so that the restrictions $H_1:B_\pm\to D_\pm$ are diffeomorphisms with the same boundary restriction $H_1|_S:S\to E$. Thus the ball identifications are compatible on their boundary and on a common two-sided collar of that boundary.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice-principle-for-foliation-pair]]). Let $S$ be an oriented Hausdorff $C^2$ surface without boundary, possibly disconnected. Then:

1. Every compact subset $K\subset S$ lies in the interior of a compact finitely cellulated $C^2$ subsurface $N$. If $K$ is contained in one connected component of $S$, $N$ can be chosen connected. A specified finite embedded regular $C^2$ graph contained in $\operatorname{Int}N$ can be included in its one-skeleton.
2. Every connected closed compact subsurface has an oriented genus normal form: the sphere for $g=0$, or the polygon word $\prod_{i=1}^g a_i b_i a_i^{-1}b_i^{-1}$ for $g\ge1$, with $\chi=2-2g$. A connected compact subsurface with $b>0$ boundary circles has a free fundamental group; capping its boundaries defines genus $g$ and gives $\chi=2-2g-b$ and free rank $2g+b-1$.
3. The fundamental group of every connected component of $S$ is torsion-free.
4. Every regular embedded $C^2$ nullhomotopic circle $c$ bounds an embedded compact disk region in $S$. Here a disk region is a compact subsurface homeomorphic to the closed disk, with boundary exactly $c$; its inherited surface structure and boundary are $C^2$. It is unique unless the **connected component containing $c$** is a sphere; in that component the two complementary disk regions are the two possibilities.

The normal forms in clause 2 are homeomorphism normal forms. No general differentiable smoothing theorem or arbitrary-surface triangulation-existence theorem is a premise of this item.

Assume countable choice. For $n=2$ or $3$, a smoothly embedded closed $n$-ball in a connected boundaryless smooth $n$-manifold can be carried to a sufficiently small coordinate round ball by a smooth ambient isotopy. Consequently, a smooth closed disk in the boundary of a smooth $3$-ball is a standard disk window: the pair consisting of the ball and that disk is diffeomorphic to a round ball with a hemispherical boundary disk. Attaching a smooth $3$-ball to a smooth manifold along one such disk window does not change the diffeomorphism type, after smoothing the corner. The same conclusion holds in reverse, when a ball meeting the boundary in one disk is removed; the diffeomorphism is supported near the attached or removed ball and its attaching collar.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$.

1. **Compact main case.** Let $M$ be a compact smooth manifold, possibly with boundary, let $N$ be a smooth manifold without boundary, let $F:M\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings that is constant near the ends of $I$, and let $W$ be an open neighbourhood of $F(M\times I)$ in $N$. Then there is an ambient isotopy $H:N\times I\to N$ with $H_0=\mathrm{id}_N$, every $H_t$ a diffeomorphism, $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ for all $t\in I$, $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ outside $W$ for every $t$, and $H_t$ stationary near the ends; if $F$ is constant near the ends with parameter $\varepsilon$, then $H_t=\mathrm{id}_N$ for $t\le\varepsilon/2$ and $H_t=H_1$ for $t\ge1-\varepsilon/2$.
2. **Relative form.** Let $N$ be boundaryless, $U\subseteq N$ open, $A\subseteq U$ compact, and let $F:U\times I\to N$ be a smooth isotopy of embeddings whose track image is open in $N\times I$. Then there is a compactly supported ambient isotopy $H$ of $N$ with $H_t\circ F_0=F_t$ on a neighbourhood of $A$ for every $t$.
3. **Boundary stratum.** If $N$ has boundary and $F(M\times I)\subseteq\partial N$, then the ambient isotopy of clause 1 can be chosen with every $H_t$ carrying $\partial N$ onto itself; if $F(M\times I)\subseteq N\setminus\partial N$, it can be chosen compactly supported in $N\setminus\partial N$.
4. **General isotopies.** For the same compact source (possibly with boundary) and boundaryless target as in clause 1, every smooth isotopy extends with support in a compact subset of any prescribed neighbourhood $W$ of $F(M\times I)$. The endpoint-constancy hypothesis and the stationary-end conclusion are both omitted; all other conclusions of clause 1 hold.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: A sphere transverse to a closed link has an even number of intersection points with each link component. By [F2] its two sides are distinct open balls; along a parametrized link circle a transverse boundary crossing switches the side. Returning to the starting point requires an even number of switches. This applies equally after small corner roundings supported away from $L$.

By [F3] the circle $c$ bounds two disks on $S$. They cannot each contain one of the two punctures. If they did, joining either to $D$ and rounding along $c$ would give a sphere meeting $L$ exactly once, contrary to step 1.1. Thus one of the two disks, denoted $E$, contains no puncture. The union $E\cup D$, after rounding, is a sphere disjoint from $L$. By [F1] and [F2] one of its closed ball sides, denoted $V$, contains no link points.

Perform the usual two-copy disk surgery along $D$: cut a thin annular collar of $c$ from $S$, cap its two sides by nearby disjoint copies of $D$, and round. It gives disjoint spheres $S_0,S_1$, where $S_0$ is the rounded $E\cup D$ and $S_1$ is the disk-replacement sphere containing both original punctures. The ball $V$ from step 2.1 may be adjusted by the same small collar push, remaining disjoint from $L$. The connected sphere $S_1$ is disjoint from $\partial V=S_0$ and contains link points outside $V$, so it lies entirely outside $V$. Thus $\operatorname{int}V\cap S_1=\varnothing$.

Reversing this two-copy surgery joins $S_0$ to $S_1$ by the short tube in the product neighborhood of $D$ and recovers $S$. Absorb that short joining collar into $V$. The result is an embedded ball $V'$ meeting $S_1$ just in one disk window and disjoint from the rest of $S_1$; adjoining a short disk collar to a ball is the elementary disk absorption in [F4]. Its interior and a sufficiently small neighborhood are disjoint from $L$. Replacing the window of $S_1$ by the other boundary disk of $V'$ recovers the original sphere, up to the arbitrarily small corner choices. The retained punctured disk $S\setminus\operatorname{int}E$ is outside this window.

This empty ball bulge is removed by an isotopy, not merely by a diffeomorphism assertion. Use the standard ball-window coordinates of [F4], retaining the window's disk coordinates and extending them across its collar. In these coordinates the bulged disk is the graph $t=\gamma(x)$ over a planar disk, where $\gamma\ge0$ is smooth and vanishes on a collar of the disk boundary; the unbulged disk is $t=0$. This is the thin-cap representation obtained by flattening one window collar and rounding its edge. The graphs $t=(1-u)\gamma(x)$, $0\le u\le1$, give a smooth isotopy of the whole sphere, fixed outside the window, because each graph remains embedded and agrees with the fixed sphere near the window boundary. Its compact track lies in the link-free ball neighborhood. Extend it by [F5], with support there. The resulting ambient isotopy fixes $L$ pointwise and carries the original sphere to the disk-replacement sphere.

The two-copy and graph constructions permit all their collar widths to be arbitrarily small. Hence the final replacement disk can lie arbitrarily close to $D$, and the final sphere equals the original retained punctured disk outside a small collar of $c$. The punctures were fixed throughout. The ambient isotopy carries each ball side together with its entire link tangle, so a boundary-parallel arc disk and the absence or presence of closed components transport in both directions. Thus side-tangle nontriviality is preserved as asserted.

citations.quote:
A **2-tangle diagram** is a regular diagram in a disk of two properly embedded tangle arcs and possibly finitely many closed tangle components, with four specified endpoints on the disk boundary; the arcs and circles are disjoint in the represented 3-ball, while their projections may have crossings. A **flyping circle** is a simple closed curve in the projection sphere whose intersection with the diagram consists of exactly three points, exactly one of which is a crossing; the circle is transverse to both branches at that crossing and to the diagram at the other two points. A small annular neighborhood of this circle has two complementary tangle disks. A **flype** fixes the tangle in one disk, interchanges which pair of strands crosses in the annular neighborhood, and turns over the tangle in the other disk: its projected tangle is reflected and all its over-under crossing data are reversed. This turnover is a half-turn in three-dimensional space about an axis in the projection sphere. Component orientations are transported by this motion, and the exterior diagram is fixed. The move with the opposite choice of fixed disk is also allowed; a disk containing no crossings is allowed. A flype whose fixed tangle has no crossings is called an **entire flype**. Diagrams are drawn on the oriented projection sphere; a **sphere planar isotopy** is an orientation-preserving smooth isotopy of that sphere carrying the decorated diagram. A plane diagram is obtained by choosing a point of the sphere outside the projection and deleting it. At each crossing of a link diagram, a **crossing ball** is a small 3-ball in which the overpass lies on the upper hemisphere and the underpass lies on the lower hemisphere, with the rest of the link outside that ball. Replacing all crossing disks by upper hemispheres or by lower hemispheres gives the shifted projection spheres $S_+$ and $S_-$. A **saddle disk** in a crossing ball is a properly embedded disk whose boundary meets each of the two hemispheres in two arcs and whose interior passes across the equatorial crossing disk. For a closed embedded surface transverse to the link and to $S_+$ and $S_-$, each component $C$ of its intersection with either shifted sphere has a **bubble word**: read once around $C$, recording $P$ each time it crosses the link and $S$ each time it passes through a crossing ball along a saddle disk. The surface is in **bubble standard position** if every such word is nonempty and no word records the same crossing ball more than once. A **Conway sphere** is an embedded sphere meeting the link transversely in four points; it is in crossing-ball standard position when its intersection with the crossing balls consists of saddle disks and its shifted-sphere intersection curves satisfy the bubble-standard conditions.

The turnover convention is the one in Kindred's Definition 2.9 and Figure 1. In particular, an entire flype permits viewing the whole diagram from the opposite side of the sphere, as in his Definition 2.11. Closed components inside a tangle disk are carried along with its arcs.
Every nonempty subset $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ has a least element: there is $\ell \in S$ with $\ell \le s$ for all $s \in S$.

Assume countable choice. Let $B$ be a supplied smooth closed $3$-ball and let $F\subset B$ be a compact neatly properly embedded smooth surface, possibly disconnected, with no closed components. If at least one component of $F$ is not a disk, there exists an embedded disk $X\subset\operatorname{int}B$ such that $X\cap F=\partial X$ and $\partial X$ does not bound a disk in $F$. The assertion concerns a geometric compressing disk for the whole surface; it does not require specifying its boundary component in advance.

Assume countable choice. Let $L\subset S^3$ be a nonsplit smooth link and let $S\subset S^3$ be a smooth sphere meeting $L$ transversely in two points. Let $D$ be an embedded disk with $\partial D=c\subset S\setminus L$ and $\operatorname{int}D\cap(S\cup L)=\varnothing$. Assume the disk meets $S$ transversely along its boundary collar.

Then $c$ bounds a disk $E\subset S\setminus L$. Replacing $E$ by $D$, with a small collar push and corner rounding near $c$, gives a sphere $S'$ ambient isotopic to $S$ by an isotopy fixing $L$ pointwise. The endpoint sphere agrees with $S$ outside $E$ and an arbitrarily small collar of $c$, and its new disk lies in an arbitrarily small neighborhood of $D$. In particular the two punctures and the nontriviality of either side tangle are preserved.

derivations.claim: Call the spheres satisfying all the stated geometric conditions admissible. This class is nonempty because it contains $S_0$. Each admissible sphere has finite $s(S)$ by hypothesis and finite $c(S)$: its transverse intersections with a compact boundary sphere form a compact one-manifold, hence finitely many circles. Apply [F2] first to the nonempty set of saddle counts and then to the cut-circle counts among spheres with the least saddle count. Choose a sphere attaining these two minima. It minimizes $(s,c)$ in lexicographic order, without requiring a simultaneous choice from an infinite family of witnesses.

For either sign, $F_\pm=S\cap B_\pm$ is a compact neat proper surface by the supplied corner conventions. Every component has boundary. Indeed a closed component would be an entire connected component of the sphere $S$, since it is open in $S$ and compact, so it would equal $S$. But $S$ meets $L$ outside the open ball, and transversality to the boundary ensures that a sphere touching that boundary also has points on its other side. Thus the whole sphere cannot be contained in $B_\pm$ as a closed piece.

Suppose $F_+$ has a nondisk component. By [F3] there is an embedded disk $D\subset\operatorname{int}B_+$ whose boundary $a$ lies in the interior of $F_+$, whose interior misses $F_+$ and whose boundary does not bound a disk in $F_+$. The disk's interior also misses the rest of $S$, because that rest is outside $\operatorname{int}B_+$. It misses $L$, every $C_j$, and both boundary spheres. The last assertion follows from $D\subset\operatorname{int}B_+$ and the stated disjointness properties. Apply [F4] to obtain the puncture-free sphere disk $E\subset S$ bounded by $a$.

The disk $E$ contains at least one component of $S\cap\partial B_+$. Otherwise, since its boundary lies in $\operatorname{int}B_+$, its connected interior would stay in $\operatorname{int}B_+$ and it would be a disk in $F_+$ bounded by $a$, contradicting step 3.1. Every cut circle that meets $E$ lies entirely in its interior, because $\partial E=a$ misses both boundary spheres. Likewise, each saddle component of $S\cap C_j$ either lies wholly inside $E$ or misses its interior: it is connected and cannot cross $a$, which is outside every $C_j$. Thus removing $E$ removes whole cut circles and whole saddle patches.

Use [F4] to replace $E$ by a nearby copy of $D$. The copy and its rounding collar can be kept inside $\operatorname{int}B_+$, since the compact disk $D$ is disjoint from its boundary, from the other boundary sphere and from every crossing ball. The new sphere $S'$ therefore adds no cut circle and no saddle patch. Its retained part is unchanged near all these sets, while step 4.1 removes at least one cut circle and possibly some saddle disks. Its two link punctures remain fixed. It is consequently admissible, with $s(S')\le s(S)$ and $c(S')<c(S)$. If the saddle count decreases, the first coordinate decreases; otherwise the second coordinate decreases. Either case contradicts the joint minimum in step 1.1.

Hence every component of $F_+$ is a disk. The identical argument with the signs exchanged treats $F_-$, because the geometric disjointness assumptions are symmetric. Both conclusions hold simultaneously for the same minimizing sphere.
